stem: What does prefixing an environment variable with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` do in a Next.js app?

options.text: It encrypts the value so that only Server Components can read it
options.why: There is no encryption; the prefix is about exposing a value, not protecting it.

options.text: It inlines the value into the browser bundle at build time
options.why: Next.js replaces `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_*` references with the build-time value, so the browser can use it.

options.text: It makes the value readable at runtime from the hosting dashboard
options.why: Public values are frozen at build time; changing them at runtime has no effect on the client.

options.text: It loads the variable only from `.env.production` files
options.why: The prefix does not change which `.env*` file a variable comes from.

explanation: Variables without the prefix stay on the server. Adding `NEXT_PUBLIC_` tells Next.js to inline the value into the JavaScript sent to the browser during `next build`. That makes it public, so never put secrets behind this prefix, and remember the value is fixed when the build runs.

stem: In a Next.js app, a `'use client'` component can read `process.env.DB_PASSWORD` (a variable without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix) and get its real value in the browser.

options.text: True
options.why: Server-only variables are never sent to the browser, so the client sees undefined.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: only `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables are inlined for the browser; others exist only in the Node.js environment.

explanation: Non-prefixed variables are available only on the server. In a Client Component running in the browser, `process.env.DB_PASSWORD` is `undefined`. This is what keeps secrets such as database passwords out of the client bundle.

stem: Which of these file names can Next.js NOT load as its configuration file?

options.text: `next.config.ts`
options.why: TypeScript config is supported; export a `NextConfig` object.

options.text: `next.config.mjs`
options.why: The `.mjs` form is the documented way to write the config as an ES module.

options.text: `next.config.cjs`
options.why: The docs state that `.cjs` and `.cts` config files are currently not supported.

options.text: `next.config.js`
options.why: This is the original, fully supported config file name.

explanation: Next.js reads `next.config.js`, `next.config.mjs` and `next.config.ts`. Config files with the `.cjs` or `.cts` extensions are not supported, which surprises teams that rename files to force CommonJS in a `"type": "module"` package.

stem: You set `output: 'export'` in `next.config.ts` and run `next build`. Which folder holds the generated HTML, CSS and JS files? Type the folder name.
explanation: A static export writes its files to the `out` folder, with one HTML file per route (for example `out/index.html` and `out/404.html`). Any static host such as Nginx or S3 can then serve that folder.

stem: Match each `next.config.js` option with what it controls.

options.text: Gzip compression of rendered content and static files under `next start`
options.why: This is `compress`, on by default.

options.text: Generating an ETag for every page
options.why: This is `generateEtags`, on by default.

options.text: The folder `next build` writes to instead of `.next`
options.why: This is `distDir`, which must stay inside the project.

options.text: Opting the app into React Strict Mode
options.why: This is `reactStrictMode`, already `true` by default for the App Router.

explanation: `compress` (default on) gzips responses when you run `next start` or a custom server; turn it off only when something in front, such as nginx with Brotli, already compresses. `generateEtags` (default on) adds an ETag to every page, and you can disable it if your cache strategy for HTML differs. `distDir` renames the build output folder from `.next`, and it must not point outside the project directory. `reactStrictMode` turns on React Strict Mode; since Next.js 13.5.1 it is already `true` by default with the App Router.
reference: Next.js docs: next.config.js (compress, generateEtags, distDir, reactStrictMode)

stem: What is the minimum Node.js version required by Next.js 16?

options.text: Node.js 18.17
options.why: That was the Next.js 15 minimum; Node.js 18 is no longer supported in 16.

options.text: Node.js 20.9
options.why: The upgrade guide lists 20.9.0 (LTS) as the new minimum.

options.text: Node.js 22.0
options.why: Node.js 22 works, but it is not the minimum.

options.text: Node.js 16.14
options.why: Node.js 16 has been unsupported for several major versions.

explanation: Next.js 16 raises the minimum to Node.js 20.9.0 and drops Node.js 18. It also requires TypeScript 5.1+ and targets Chrome, Edge and Firefox 111+ and Safari 16.4+.

stem: You need to serve a Next.js app under `https://example.com/docs` instead of the domain root. Which `next.config` option sets that path prefix? Type the option name.
explanation: `basePath: '/docs'` prefixes every route, and `next/link` adds it automatically, so `/about` becomes `/docs/about`. The value is inlined into client bundles at build time, so changing it requires a rebuild.

stem: A project upgraded to Next.js 16 still has `"lint": "next lint"` in `package.json`. What happens?

options.text: It works, but prints a deprecation warning
options.why: The command was not merely deprecated; it was removed.

options.text: It fails, because `next lint` was removed
options.why: Next.js 16 removed `next lint`; use the ESLint or Biome CLI directly.

options.text: It runs Biome instead of ESLint automatically
options.why: Next.js does not swap linters for you.

options.text: It runs, and `next build` also lints as before
options.why: `next build` no longer runs linting in Next.js 16.

explanation: Next.js 16 removed the `next lint` command and the `eslint` option in the config, and `next build` no longer lints. Run ESLint (flat config) or Biome directly; a codemod can migrate the script.

stem: A Client Component calls `fetch(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL + '/orders')`. Ops change `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` in the container's environment and restart it without rebuilding. Browsers keep calling the old URL. Why?

options.text: The browser cached the old environment in `localStorage`
options.why: Next.js does not store environment variables in browser storage.

options.text: Containers read `.env` files only on the first start
options.why: Restarts would re-read env, but that is not the issue for browser code.

options.text: The value was inlined into the JS bundle at build time
options.why: Public variables are replaced during `next build`; only a rebuild picks up the new value.

options.text: Client Components must read env vars through `useEnv()`
options.why: There is no such hook; inlining happens at build time.

explanation: During `next build`, every `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` reference is replaced with the literal value. After that the app no longer reacts to changes in that variable. To change it you must rebuild, or read the value on the server at request time and pass it down.

stem: With `NODE_ENV=development`, Next.js looks a variable up in several places and stops at the first match. Put them in lookup order, first checked to last.

options.text: `process.env`
options.why: Values already in the real environment win.

options.text: `.env.development.local`
options.why: Environment-specific local overrides.

options.text: `.env.local`
options.why: Local overrides for all environments except test.

options.text: `.env.development`
options.why: Shared defaults for development.

options.text: `.env`
options.why: Shared defaults for every environment.

explanation: The order is `process.env`, then `.env.$(NODE_ENV).local`, `.env.local`, `.env.$(NODE_ENV)` and finally `.env`. So a variable exported in the shell beats every file, and `.env.development.local` beats a value in `.env`.

stem: Your test runner sets `NODE_ENV=test` and loads variables the same way Next.js does. `API_KEY` is defined only in `.env.local`, yet tests see `undefined`. Why?

options.text: `.env.local` is only read by `next build`
options.why: It is read by dev and production; test is the exception.

options.text: `.env.local` is skipped when `NODE_ENV` is `test`
options.why: Tests should give the same results for everyone, so local overrides are ignored.

options.text: Test mode reads only variables prefixed with `TEST_`
options.why: There is no such prefix rule.

options.text: Variables are never loaded when `NODE_ENV` is `test`
options.why: `.env.test` and `.env` are still loaded in test.

explanation: In the test environment Next.js loads `.env.test`, `.env.test.local` and `.env`, but deliberately not `.env.local`, so tests do not depend on one developer's machine. Put test defaults in `.env.test`, which belongs in the repository.

stem: Which of these references are replaced with literal values at build time? (Choose two.)

options.text: `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID` written out in full
options.why: A direct, static reference to a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable is inlined.

options.text: `process.env[name]` with `name = 'NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID'`
options.why: Dynamic lookups with a variable key are not inlined.

options.text: `const env = process.env; env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID`
options.why: Going through an alias of `process.env` defeats inlining.

options.text: `process.env.customKey` declared in the config `env` option
options.why: Values in `next.config` `env` are always inlined into the bundle.

options.text: `const { NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID } = process.env`
options.why: Destructuring is not a static reference, so it is not replaced.

explanation: Inlining is a find-and-replace on the exact expression `process.env.NAME`. Direct references to `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables and to keys from the config `env` option are replaced. Computed keys, aliases of `process.env` and destructuring are left alone, so in the browser they read `undefined`.

stem: You deploy with `output: 'standalone'` and start `node .next/standalone/server.js`. HTML loads, but every CSS and JS file under `/_next/static/` returns 404. What did you miss?

options.text: Running `next start` instead of the standalone `server.js`
options.why: `server.js` is the intended entry point for standalone output.

options.text: Copying `.next/static` and `public` alongside it
options.why: The minimal server does not copy these folders; you must copy them yourself.

options.text: Setting `assetPrefix` to the server's own URL
options.why: An asset prefix is for CDNs and does not create missing files.

options.text: Installing `node_modules` next to `server.js` after the build
options.why: Standalone output already includes the traced dependencies it needs.

explanation: Standalone output copies only the traced server files. The `public` and `.next/static` folders are left out because a CDN would usually serve them. Copy them after the build: `cp -r public .next/standalone/ && cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/`.

stem: After upgrading to Next.js 16, `next build` fails because a `webpack` configuration was found, added by a plugin. Which actions resolve it? (Choose three.)

options.text: Build with `next build --webpack` to keep using Webpack
options.why: The flag opts out of the default Turbopack build.

options.text: Migrate the Webpack options to Turbopack equivalents
options.why: Switching fully to Turbopack removes the conflict.

options.text: Run `next build --turbopack` to use Turbopack and ignore the config
options.why: This builds with Turbopack and ignores the `webpack` function.

options.text: Move the options into `experimental.turbopack`
options.why: In 16 the Turbopack config moved to a top-level `turbopack` key.

options.text: Downgrade Node.js so that Webpack becomes the default again
options.why: The bundler default does not depend on the Node.js version.

explanation: Turbopack is the default for `next build` in Next.js 16, and the build fails when it finds a `webpack` config so that it is not silently ignored. Choose explicitly: `--webpack`, `--turbopack`, or migrate the config. Turbopack options now live in the top-level `turbopack` key.

stem: Setting `assetPrefix: 'https://cdn.example.com'` makes Next.js serve files from the `public` folder through the CDN as well.

options.text: True
options.why: `assetPrefix` covers `/_next/static` only, not `public` files.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: files in `public` keep their normal URLs unless you add the prefix yourself.

explanation: `assetPrefix` applies to the JavaScript and CSS that Next.js loads from `/_next/`, which comes from `.next/static`. Files in `public` are not affected. To serve them from a CDN you must add the prefix to those URLs yourself. On Vercel you do not need an asset prefix at all, because a CDN is configured automatically.

stem: A Next.js 15 app reads values from `serverRuntimeConfig` and `publicRuntimeConfig`. What should it use after upgrading to 16?

options.text: The same options, moved under `experimental`
options.why: They were removed, not moved to `experimental`.

options.text: A new `runtimeConfig` key that merges the server and public objects
options.why: No such replacement key exists.

options.text: Environment variables, with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` for client values
options.why: Next.js 16 removed runtime config in favour of plain environment variables.

options.text: The `env` option, which is read fresh on every request
options.why: The `env` option is inlined at build time, not read per request.

explanation: Both runtime config options were removed in Next.js 16. Server code reads `process.env` directly; to make sure a value is read at request time rather than at build, call `await connection()` first. Values the browser needs use the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix.

stem: A static export has `trailingSlash: true`. What file does the `/about` page produce?

options.text: `out/about.html`
options.why: That is the default naming without `trailingSlash`.

options.text: `out/about/index.html`
options.why: With `trailingSlash: true`, each page becomes a folder with an index file.

options.text: `out/about/page.html`
options.why: Next.js never names exported files `page.html`.

options.text: `out/_next/about.html`
options.why: `_next` holds static assets, not page HTML.

explanation: By default a static export writes `/about` as `about.html`. With `trailingSlash: true` it writes `about/index.html`, which matches how many static hosts resolve `/about/`. The same option also makes the server redirect `/about` to `/about/`.

stem: When does Next.js call the `register` function exported from `instrumentation.ts`?

options.text: Before every incoming request is handled
options.why: It runs once per server instance, not per request.

options.text: Once per server instance, before it serves requests
options.why: Next.js waits for `register` to finish before serving traffic.

options.text: Only during `next build`, while pages are prerendered
options.why: It runs when a server instance starts, not only at build time.

options.text: The first time a Client Component hydrates in the browser
options.why: That would be client instrumentation, a separate file.

explanation: `register` runs once when a new Next.js server instance starts and must complete before the server handles requests, which makes it the place to initialise OpenTelemetry or other observability tools. It can be async. The same file may export `onRequestError` to report server errors.

stem: Instead of setting `deploymentId` in `next.config`, which environment variable can provide the deployment ID? Type its name.
explanation: `NEXT_DEPLOYMENT_ID` sets the deployment ID. If both are present, the `deploymentId` value in `next.config` takes precedence. The ID powers version-skew protection during rolling deployments.

stem: You promote one Docker image from staging to production and set `API_URL` differently in each. A Server Component page reads `process.env.API_URL`, but production still shows the staging URL. The build output marked the route `○`. What fixes it?

options.text: Rename the variable to `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`
options.why: That inlines it at build time, which is the opposite of what you need.

options.text: Call `await connection()` before reading the variable
options.why: This makes the read happen at request time, so each environment's value is used.

options.text: Move the value into `.env.production.local`
options.why: The page was still prerendered at build, so the file would not be re-read.

options.text: Set `NODE_ENV=production` in the production container
options.why: The mode is already production; the issue is when the page renders.

explanation: A `○` route is fully prerendered during `next build`, so any `process.env` read inside it is evaluated once, with the build environment's values. Reading the variable after `await connection()` (or another request-time API) renders it on demand, which is what lets one image move between environments.

stem: Which features break when you switch an App Router project to `output: 'export'`? (Choose three.)

options.text: Server Actions
options.why: They need a server to receive the POST requests.

options.text: Client Components that fetch data with SWR
options.why: Client-side fetching works in a static export.

options.text: A `proxy.ts` that redirects by cookie
options.why: Proxy needs the incoming request, which a static host never runs.

options.text: Image optimization with the default `next/image` loader
options.why: It needs a server; use a custom loader instead.

options.text: Dynamic routes that list every param in `generateStaticParams`
options.why: Known params are prerendered to HTML files.

options.text: A `GET` Route Handler that returns static JSON
options.why: It is rendered to a static file during the build.

explanation: A static export produces HTML, CSS and JS files only, so anything that needs a running server is unsupported: Server Actions, Proxy, cookies, rewrites, redirects, headers, ISR, Draft Mode, intercepting routes and default image optimization. Client-side fetching, fully listed dynamic routes and request-independent `GET` handlers still work.

stem: Four containers run behind a load balancer, and each container runs `next build` when it starts. Users intermittently get "Failed to find Server Action" when submitting forms. What is the root cause?

options.text: Server Actions only work with a single instance
options.why: They work across instances when the instances agree on keys and builds.

options.text: The load balancer strips the `Next-Action` header
options.why: That would fail every time, not intermittently by instance.

options.text: Every build makes its own encryption key
options.why: An action from one instance can't be decrypted by another unless the key is shared.

options.text: The form is missing a `deploymentId` hidden field
options.why: Deployment IDs are not sent as form fields.

explanation: Next.js encrypts Server Function closure variables with a key generated per build. Separate builds mean separate keys, so a form rendered by one container fails on another. Build once and ship the same artifact, and set the same `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (base64, 16, 24 or 32 bytes) on every instance.

stem: Three self-hosted instances serve an ISR page. An editor publishes, and an API calls `revalidatePath('/blog')`, which reaches one instance. For a while, users get different versions depending on the instance. Why?

options.text: `revalidatePath` only works on Vercel
options.why: It works self-hosted; the cache scope is the problem.

options.text: Each instance keeps its own cache on its local disk
options.why: Revalidating one instance does not touch the others' caches.

options.text: ISR needs `output: 'standalone'` to stay consistent
options.why: The output mode does not decide where the cache lives.

options.text: The page needs `force-dynamic` to use revalidation
options.why: Forcing dynamic rendering would disable ISR altogether.

explanation: By default the server cache used by ISR lives in memory and on each instance's own disk. Invalidating it on one instance leaves the others serving stale pages until they revalidate themselves. Configure a shared `cacheHandler` (for example backed by Redis), often with `cacheMaxMemorySize: 0`, and implement tag coordination such as `refreshTags()` for tag-based invalidation.

stem: During rolling deployments, some users who keep a tab open get errors loading JavaScript chunks after the new version goes live. Which `next.config` setting addresses this?

options.text: `generateBuildId` returning `Date.now()`
options.why: A changing build ID per build does nothing to reconcile old clients.

options.text: `assetPrefix` pointing at a CDN
options.why: A CDN still won't have the old chunks once they are replaced.

options.text: `compress: false` to avoid cached gzip files
options.why: Compression has nothing to do with missing chunks.

options.text: `deploymentId` set to a per-deployment value
options.why: On a mismatch, Next.js switches to a full page reload instead of client navigation.

explanation: This is version skew: an old client asks for assets or Server Functions that the new deployment no longer has. With `deploymentId` set, asset URLs carry `?dpl=<id>` and navigation requests carry an `x-deployment-id` header. When the client detects a mismatch it performs a hard navigation, loading a consistent version at the cost of in-memory state.

stem: Put these steps of a multi-stage Docker build for `output: 'standalone'` in order.

options.text: Install dependencies with `npm ci` in a builder stage
options.why: Dependencies are needed to build.

options.text: Copy the source and run `next build`
options.why: Produces `.next/standalone` and `.next/static`.

options.text: In the runner stage, copy `.next/standalone` into the app folder
options.why: This holds `server.js` and the traced `node_modules`.

options.text: Copy `.next/static` to `.next/static` inside the app folder
options.why: The minimal server does not include static assets.

options.text: Start the server with `node server.js`
options.why: The standalone server replaces `next start`.

explanation: Build in one stage, then copy only what the runtime needs into a slim runner stage: the standalone folder, plus `.next/static` and `public`, which standalone output does not include. Start with `node server.js` and set `PORT` and `HOSTNAME` as needed.

stem: A self-hosted App Router site uses `loading.tsx` and Suspense, but behind nginx the whole page arrives at once instead of streaming. Which changes help? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disable proxy buffering, for example with `X-Accel-Buffering: no`
options.why: nginx buffers the whole response unless buffering is turned off.

options.text: Ensure the load balancer passes chunked responses through
options.why: Any buffering hop in front of Next.js defeats streaming.

options.text: Switch to `output: 'standalone'`
options.why: The output mode does not change how responses are streamed.

options.text: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` to the page
options.why: That stops request-time rendering instead of fixing buffering.

options.text: Move the Suspense boundaries into Client Components
options.why: Streaming is decided by the infrastructure here, not by component type.

explanation: Next.js streams self-hosted responses fine, but every proxy or load balancer in between must pass chunks through without buffering. With nginx, disable buffering (for example by sending `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), and check that the load balancer supports chunked transfer or HTTP/2 streaming. Without that, Partial Prerendering also loses its fast first byte.

stem: In a monorepo, `apps/web` imports code from `packages/shared` that reads a JSON file at runtime. With `output: 'standalone'`, the deployed server crashes because the file is missing. What is the right fix?

options.text: Add `packages/shared` to `transpilePackages`
options.why: That changes compilation, not which files are traced into the output.

options.text: Copy `node_modules` from the monorepo root into the image
options.why: It bloats the image and defeats standalone output's purpose.

options.text: Set `outputFileTracingRoot` to the monorepo root
options.why: Tracing then includes files outside the app folder.

options.text: Set `distDir` to a folder at the monorepo root
options.why: Moving the build folder does not change what is traced.

explanation: File tracing starts from the Next.js project folder by default, so files above `apps/web` are not included. Pointing `outputFileTracingRoot` at the monorepo root (for example `path.join(__dirname, '../../')`) lets tracing pick them up. Use `outputFileTracingIncludes` for files that tracing still misses.

stem: When do you need to add a package to `transpilePackages` in a Next.js 16 app that builds with Turbopack?

options.text: For every workspace package that the app imports in the monorepo
options.why: Turbopack transpiles workspace packages automatically.

options.text: When a `node_modules` package ships raw TypeScript or JSX
options.why: Next.js does not compile `node_modules` unless the package is listed.

options.text: For any package that uses ES modules syntax
options.why: ESM packages are handled without being listed.

options.text: For server-only packages such as database drivers
options.why: Those usually belong in `serverExternalPackages`, not here.

explanation: `transpilePackages` opts a dependency into compilation. Turbopack already transpiles workspace packages in a monorepo, so the common case is a published package that ships untranspiled TypeScript or JSX. A package cannot be listed in both `transpilePackages` and `serverExternalPackages`; the build throws at start.

stem: With `typescript: { ignoreBuildErrors: true }`, `next build` still runs the TypeScript type check but stops type errors from failing the build.

options.text: True
options.why: The option skips the type-check step entirely; nothing is run and suppressed.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it bypasses type checking completely, so you must type-check elsewhere, for example in CI.

explanation: The docs are explicit: `ignoreBuildErrors` does not run TypeScript and hide errors, it skips the check. That is why projects using it should run `tsc --noEmit` as a separate step. This repo does exactly that with its own typecheck script.

stem: A plugin's `next.config.ts` runs extra setup only when `process.argv.includes('dev')`. After upgrading to Next.js 16, the setup stops running in `next dev`. Why, and what should it check instead?

options.text: `next dev` now passes `--development` instead of `dev` in argv
options.why: The command is still `next dev`; the config loading changed.

options.text: Config files no longer run in development at all
options.why: The config is still loaded during development.

options.text: The config is now bundled, so `process` is undefined
options.why: Config files are not bundled, so `process` is still available.

options.text: Config now loads only in the server process; check `phase`
options.why: The CLI process no longer loads it, so `argv` lacks `dev` where the config runs.

explanation: Next.js 16 stopped loading the config twice in development. It is now loaded only when the dev server starts, where `process.argv` no longer includes `dev`, although `build` and `typegen` still appear for those commands. Use the `phase` argument of a function-style config, or check `NODE_ENV === 'development'`.

stem: Match each kind of response with the `Cache-Control` header a self-hosted Next.js server sets on it.

options.text: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`
options.why: For content-hashed files.

options.text: `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate`
options.why: For user-specific output.

options.text: `s-maxage=<revalidate>, stale-while-revalidate`
options.why: For pages that revalidate.

options.text: `no-transform, max-age=60`
options.why: Not a header Next.js sets by default.

prompts.text: A page that calls `cookies()` while rendering
An ISR page with a revalidation time

explanation: Truly immutable assets carry a SHA hash in their file name, so they get a one-year `immutable` header that cannot be overridden. Dynamically rendered pages are marked private and uncacheable so that user data never lands in a shared cache. ISR pages use `s-maxage` with `stale-while-revalidate`.

stem: You are adding locale-prefixed routes such as `/fr/products` to an App Router app. Which steps match the documented approach? (Choose two.)

options.text: Nest the special files under an `app/[lang]` segment
options.why: Every layout and page then receives the `lang` param.

options.text: Detect the locale in Proxy, for example from `Accept-Language`
options.why: Proxy redirects requests without a locale to the right prefix.

options.text: Add an `i18n: { locales, defaultLocale }` block to `next.config`
options.why: That config is Pages Router only; the App Router has no built-in i18n routing.

options.text: Set `basePath` to the user's locale at runtime
options.why: `basePath` is fixed at build time and applies to the whole app.

options.text: Generate one separate build per locale
options.why: A single build serves every locale through the `[lang]` segment.

explanation: The App Router does not use the `i18n` config. Instead, put routes under `app/[lang]`, pick the locale in Proxy (for example from the `Accept-Language` header) and redirect requests that lack one. Load translation dictionaries in layouts or pages based on the `lang` param.

stem: A Docker container runs `node server.js` from standalone output. You want it on port 8080, reachable from outside the container. What do you do?

options.text: Run `node server.js -p 8080 -H 0.0.0.0`
options.why: Those are `next start` flags; the standalone server reads environment variables.

options.text: Set `port: 8080` in `next.config.ts` before building
options.why: There is no `port` config option.

options.text: Set `PORT=8080` and `HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0` env vars
options.why: The standalone `server.js` reads both variables at startup.

options.text: Add `EXPOSE 8080` to the Dockerfile and nothing else
options.why: `EXPOSE` documents a port; it does not change where the server listens.

explanation: The minimal `server.js` is a plain Node script, so CLI flags such as `-p` do not apply. It reads the `PORT` and `HOSTNAME` environment variables, for example `PORT=8080 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 node server.js`. Binding to `0.0.0.0` makes it reachable through the container's published port.

stem: A self-hosted team sets both `deploymentId: process.env.GIT_SHA` and a custom `generateBuildId` that returns the date. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The build ID from `generateBuildId` is used for skew detection
options.why: Skew is detected from the deployment ID when it is set.

options.text: `generateBuildId` is ignored when a deployment ID is set
options.why: With a deployment ID, Next.js uses a constant build ID.

options.text: Both IDs must match, or the build fails
options.why: They are not compared, and no such build error exists.

options.text: The deployment ID is ignored unless `NEXT_DEPLOYMENT_ID` is set
options.why: The config value works on its own and wins over the variable.

explanation: When `deploymentId` is configured, Next.js uses a constant build ID, `generateBuildId` stops having any effect, and version skew is detected from the deployment ID. `generateBuildId` matters only when you rebuild per environment without a deployment ID and need every container to agree.

stem: A `.env` file contains `DB_PASSWORD=pa$word` (no quotes, no escape). The app fails to connect to the database. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Unquoted values with symbols are rejected, so the variable is undefined
options.why: Unquoted values load; the `$` is what changes the value.

options.text: Next.js URL-encodes `$`, so the driver receives `pa%24word`
options.why: Values are not URL-encoded when loaded.

options.text: `$word` is read as a reference to another variable, changing the value
options.why: Next.js expands `$VARIABLE` references in `.env` files.

options.text: Passwords must be stored in `.env.local`, not `.env`
options.why: Any `.env*` file can hold the value; the parsing is the problem.

explanation: Next.js expands variable references written with `$` inside `.env*` files, so `$word` is treated as a reference to a variable named `word` rather than literal text. To keep a literal dollar sign, escape it: `DB_PASSWORD=pa\$word`. Expansion is useful for composing values such as `TWITTER_URL=https://x.com/$TWITTER_USER`.

stem: You run five Next.js instances from one deployment behind a load balancer. Which must be the same on every instance for consistent behaviour? (Choose three.)

options.text: The `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`
options.why: Otherwise one instance cannot decrypt another's Server Function payloads.

options.text: The `deploymentId`
options.why: All instances of one deployment should report the same ID.

options.text: A shared cache handler for ISR and `'use cache: remote'` data
options.why: Without it, each instance caches and revalidates on its own.

options.text: The `PORT` each instance listens on
options.why: Ports are a per-container detail behind the load balancer.

options.text: A unique `deploymentId` per instance, to tell them apart
options.why: Different IDs would trigger reloads as requests hop between instances.

explanation: Multi-instance deployments need agreement on three things: the Server Functions encryption key, the deployment ID for skew detection, and a shared cache with cross-instance tag coordination. Building once and running the same artifact everywhere takes care of most of this automatically.

stem: Each deployment has its own `deploymentId`. During a rollout, old and new instances run side by side and the load balancer picks one at random for every request. Users report repeated full page reloads. Why?

options.text: The `?dpl=` query string makes URLs too long for some proxies to cache
options.why: Length is not the issue; routing is.

options.text: Next.js routes requests with `?dpl=` to the instance of that deployment
options.why: Next.js does not read `?dpl=` for routing at all.

options.text: Requests aren't routed by deployment, so every mismatch reloads
options.why: Skew protection reloads on mismatch, but the host must route by deployment.

options.text: The deployment ID must be equal across deployments
options.why: A shared ID across deployments would hide real version skew.

explanation: With a deployment ID, a client that reaches an instance from another deployment does a hard navigation. Next.js only detects skew; it does not route on `?dpl=`. If the load balancer keeps sending a client to instances of different deployments, the client keeps reloading. Use your host or CDN to route by deployment (sticky by version) during the rollout.

stem: You run `npx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest` on a Next.js 15 app that still reads `cookies()` and `params` synchronously. What else do you need to do?

options.text: Nothing: `upgrade` runs every migration codemod
options.why: The docs note that `upgrade` does not run every migration codemod.

options.text: Add `experimental.syncRequestApis: true` to keep them working
options.why: Synchronous access was removed; no flag restores it.

options.text: Also run the async Request APIs codemod
options.why: `upgrade` does not migrate synchronous `cookies()`, `headers()` or `params` usage.

options.text: Downgrade React, because sync access depends on React 18
options.why: The change is in Next.js, not React.

explanation: Next.js 15 allowed synchronous access to Request APIs temporarily; Next.js 16 removes it. The `upgrade` codemod handles things like the Turbopack config, `next lint`, middleware to proxy and `unstable_` prefixes, but you must also run the async Request APIs codemod. `next typegen` can generate `PageProps` and `LayoutProps` helpers to type the new promises.

stem: A Next.js 15 app uses `middleware.ts` with `export const config = { runtime: 'edge' }`. You rename it to `proxy.ts` during the upgrade to 16. What happens to the Edge runtime?

options.text: Proxy runs on Edge by default, so the setting is redundant
options.why: Proxy runs on Node.js, and the runtime cannot be configured.

options.text: Proxy keeps whatever runtime the `config` export declares
options.why: Proxy's runtime is fixed to Node.js.

options.text: The build fails until you add `turbopack.runtime: 'edge'`
options.why: No such option exists.

options.text: Proxy is Node.js-only; keep `middleware.ts` to stay on Edge
options.why: `middleware` is deprecated but remains the way to stay on Edge for now.

explanation: In Next.js 16, `middleware` is renamed to `proxy`, and Proxy always runs on the Node.js runtime. If you depend on the Edge runtime, keep using the deprecated `middleware` file until further Edge guidance arrives. Config flags were renamed too, for example `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize` became `skipProxyUrlNormalize`.

stem: Next.js generates its Server Functions encryption key itself when `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is not set. How many bytes long is the key it generates by default? Type a number.
explanation: The key must be base64-encoded with a valid AES key length of 16, 24 or 32 bytes, and Next.js generates 32-byte keys by default. Set the same value on every instance so that payloads encrypted by one instance can be decrypted by another.

stem: A static export (`output: 'export'`) defines a custom image loader that points `next/image` at Cloudinary. When are the images optimized?

options.text: During `next build`, and written into the `out` folder
options.why: Static export does not optimize images at build time.

options.text: At request time, by the image service the loader points to
options.why: The loader only builds URLs; the external service does the work on demand.

options.text: In the browser, by the client-side code that `next/image` ships
options.why: The browser just requests the URL the loader produced.

options.text: Never, because static exports require `unoptimized`
options.why: A custom loader is the documented way to keep optimization.

explanation: With a static export there is no Next.js server to run the default optimizer, so you either set `unoptimized` or supply a custom loader. The loader function builds URLs for an external service such as Cloudinary, and that service optimizes each image when it is requested, not during the build.

stem: A dynamic Server Component calls `await connection()` and then reads `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_FLAG`. Ops change the variable on the server and restart without rebuilding. What does the page render?

options.text: The new value, because `connection()` makes the read happen at runtime
options.why: Request-time rendering does not undo build-time inlining.

options.text: The old build-time value, because the reference was inlined
options.why: Next.js replaces `NEXT_PUBLIC_` references at build in server code too.

options.text: `undefined`, because public variables are client-only
options.why: Public variables are usable on the server as well.

options.text: A build error, because public variables are banned in Server Components
options.why: They are allowed; they are just frozen at build time.

explanation: The docs say `next build` replaces references to `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables "in the Node.js environment" as well, so the server bundle contains the literal too. Rendering at request time cannot change a value that is no longer a lookup. Use a non-prefixed variable for anything server code must read at runtime.

stem: To "keep it out of the client", a developer adds `env: { STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY }` to `next.config.ts` without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix. What is the risk?

options.text: None: without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix the value never leaves the server
options.why: The prefix rule does not apply to the `env` option.

options.text: The key becomes available only to Route Handlers
options.why: The `env` option has no per-route scoping.

options.text: The build fails because secret-looking names are blocked
options.why: Next.js does not inspect variable names this way.

options.text: `env` values are inlined wherever referenced, even client code
options.why: The `env` option always inlines, whatever the name.

explanation: The legacy `env` config option replaces `process.env.KEY` with the value at build time, and the docs warn these values are always included in the bundle where referenced. The `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix only matters for variables loaded from the environment. Keep secrets out of `env` and read them from `process.env` in server-only code.

stem: Which statements about `onRequestError` in `instrumentation.ts` are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: The error may be a React-processed copy; use `digest` to identify it
options.why: Errors from Server Components rendering can be wrapped by React.

options.text: Its context says whether the error came from render, route, action or proxy
options.why: The context carries the route type, such as `'action'` or `'proxy'`.

options.text: It also fires for errors thrown in Client Components in the browser
options.why: It tracks server errors captured by the Next.js server.

options.text: Async work started inside it is awaited for you automatically
options.why: You must await async tasks yourself, as the docs warn.

options.text: It only works in the Node.js runtime, never on Edge
options.why: Instrumentation works in both runtimes; branch on `NEXT_RUNTIME`.

explanation: `onRequestError` receives the error, read-only request details and a context describing where it happened: Server Components render, Route Handler, Server Action or Proxy. The value may not be the original thrown object, so match on `digest`. Await any async reporting, and use `process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME` to target Node.js or Edge.

stem: A deployment ID is configured. Put the steps of how Next.js handles a client from an older deployment in order.

options.text: The client makes a client-side navigation with its `x-deployment-id` header
options.why: The client announces which deployment it came from.

options.text: The server compares that ID with its own deployment ID
options.why: This is where skew is detected.

options.text: The response carries the server's ID in `x-nextjs-deployment-id`
options.why: The client learns which deployment answered.

options.text: The client sees the mismatch and does a hard navigation
options.why: A full reload fetches a consistent set of assets.

explanation: Navigation requests include `x-deployment-id`, the server compares it with its own, and responses include `x-nextjs-deployment-id`. On a mismatch the client performs a full page reload rather than a client-side navigation, so it gets assets and Server Functions from one deployment. In-memory state such as `useState` is lost in the reload.
